stances.claim: China's swarming of 200+ militia and coast-guard vessels and its prohibition of PH fishing in our own EEZ are the modern restaging of 'Might is right' -- the very Opium-Wars rule of force that Britain imposed on it via the Treaty of Nanking and other Unequal Treaties.
stances.rhetorical_move: historical-parallel inversion (the bullied has become the bully)

stances.claim: The AA's express recognition of PH sovereign rights to fish, exploit, and develop the WPS -- under UNCLOS, which China signed and is therefore legally bound to obey -- is the better adage of 'Right is might,' i.e., the rule of law; China's selective compliance with UNCLOS while ignoring the AA exposes its rule-of-force preference.

The great powers (US, Australia, France, UK) selectively invoke the AA's freedom-of-navigation provisions for their interests while not being parties to the arbitration -- a 'little ironic' inconsistency; CJ wishes they would enforce the entire AA to show consistent adherence to 'Right is might.'
stances.rhetorical_move: selective-invocation diagnosis applied even to allies
stances.confidence: asserted as principled criticism of friendly powers

stances.claim: China's defense -- that WPS issues involve land sovereignty and ownership, which only the ICJ has jurisdiction over -- has technical force, even though China refused to participate in the arbitration.

PH ownership of the land features is supported by the 1734 Murillo-Velarde map (per Carpio and Batongbacal), reinforced by the 1898 Treaty of Paris (Spain→US) and 1900 Treaty of Washington (US→PH) cessions -- a strong case to invoke before the ICJ.
stances.confidence: asserted with deference to expert authorities

stances.claim: Manila should accept China's challenge and bring the dispute to the ICJ -- only states (not private individuals or organizations) can file under the ICJ Charter, so the responsibility is the government's; this is the path consistent with 'Right is might.'
stances.rhetorical_move: policy-recommendation framed by the column's binary thesis

notable_anecdotes: The Opium-Wars historical inversion -- Britain forcibly imposed 'Might is right' on China via Nanking and other Unequal Treaties; today a 'hi-tech, militarily revitalized and economically dominant China' restages the very rule of force on its smaller Asian neighbors, becoming 'the new bully in Asia.'

The selective-invocation diagnosis applied even to allies -- 'A little ironic indeed, because these powerful countries were not parties in the arbitral proceedings and, strictly speaking, are not bound by the AA. In fact, the United States is not even a signatory to UNCLOS. Yet, they are invoking some parts thereof that are favorable to their national interest.' -- turning the column's principled standard into a critique of friends as well as adversaries.

The 1734 Murillo-Velarde map cited via Carpio and Batongbacal -- paired with the cession chain (Spain → US via the 1898 Treaty of Paris and 1900 Treaty of Washington → PH) -- as the documentary spine of the historical ownership argument.
'Au contraire' as the typical CJ pivot-marker introducing the counterargument to China's discovery-since-time-immemorial claim.
Closing one-line question -- 'Which will prevail?' -- refusing to give the answer himself but having structured the column so the answer is inescapable.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban frames the West Philippine Sea dispute as a contest between two adages -- 'Might is right' (the rule of force) and 'Right is might' (the rule of law). By swarming the WPS with more than 200 militia and coast-guard vessels and prohibiting Philippine fishing in our own EEZ, China is restaging the very rule of force that Britain imposed on it through the Opium Wars, the Treaty of Nanking, and the Unequal Treaties of the mid-1800s -- making a hi-tech, militarily revitalized, and economically dominant China the 'new bully in Asia.' He had hoped the contemporary China would, with lessons learned, instead honor the 501-page July 12, 2016 Arbitral Award, which expressly recognized Manila's exclusive right to fish and develop the WPS under UNCLOS -- a treaty China signed and is therefore legally bound to obey. He notes the 'little ironic' inconsistency that great powers (US, Australia, France, UK) -- none of them parties to the arbitration, and the US not even a signatory to UNCLOS -- selectively invoke AA-favorable provisions for freedom-of-navigation operations; he wishes they would enforce the entire AA to show consistent adherence to 'Right is might.' He fairly states China's position: WPS issues involve land ownership and sovereignty, only the ICJ has jurisdiction; China steadfastly refused to participate in the PCA proceedings. China's discovery-since-time-immemorial claim was rejected by the AA. Au contraire, Justice Antonio T. Carpio and Prof. Jay Batongbacal show that Philippine ownership is documented by the 1734 Murillo-Velarde map, reinforced by the 1898 Treaty of Paris and 1900 Treaty of Washington under which Spain ceded the islands (including the Spratlys and Scarborough) to the US, which in turn ceded them to the Philippines. If the case is strong, Manila can now accept China's challenge and bring it to the ICJ; under the ICJ Charter, only states (not private individuals or organizations) may file. 'Might is right' vs 'Right is might.' Which will prevail?
